page: Amazon Web Services m6in.24xlarge is a general-purpose instance powered by the AWS Nitro hypervisor. It features an Intel Xeon 8375C processor with 96 vCPUs (48 physical cores with hyper-threading) running at 3.5 GHz. The system is equipped with 384 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, providing a balanced 4 GB of RAM per vCPU. It does not include local storage or dedicated GPUs, relying entirely on network-attached storage.

A key differentiator of this instance is its high-performance networking, delivering a baseline network bandwidth of 150 Gbps. Benchmark data indicates strong multi-core CPU performance, placing in the top 25% for stress-ng multi-core and Geekbench multi-core tests. Memory bandwidth is also highly competitive, with large-block read and write speeds ranking in the top 25%. Cryptographic performance is exceptional, with the Passmark CPU encryption test reaching the top 10% tier, aided by hardware-accelerated instruction sets like AES and VAES.

Given its high network throughput and strong database operation benchmarks, the m6in.24xlarge is well-suited for network-intensive applications, static web serving, and database operations such as Redis. However, the lack of local NVMe storage means all disk I/O depends on EBS performance. While it handles small to medium LLM inference tasks with average efficiency, it exhibits weak performance for large-scale LLM text generation due to the absence of GPU acceleration.
description: Amazon Web Services m6in.24xlarge is a general-purpose, network-optimized instance powered by an Intel Xeon 8375C processor. It delivers 96 vCPUs, 384 GB of DDR4 memory, and a baseline network bandwidth of 150 Gbps under the Nitro hypervisor. Lacking local storage and GPUs, it relies on network-attached storage for disk operations. Benchmarks show strong multi-core CPU performance, high memory bandwidth, and top-tier cryptographic execution, supported by AVX-512 and VAES instruction sets. The instance excels in network-heavy workloads, database operations, and static web serving, though its lack of hardware acceleration makes it less suitable for large-scale language model inference.
